Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-05-08 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 mins
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood), Carlos Mendes (Zenith - Head ML Infra), Aisha Khan (Zenith - CTO), Liam O'Connor (Zenith - SRE), Mei Tan (Zenith - PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
Redwood and Zenith scoped a POC focused on capacity sizing and autoscaling for reserved GPU capacity plus burst strategy. Key success criteria: p95 token latency under 250ms for 95% of traffic, sustainable throughput of ~1.2k concurrent requests (avg 800 QPS), and cost per 1M tokens target. Agreement to run a 24-hour benchmark with Zenith's prompt set and to validate fallback policies (smaller quantized model + cache-first routing).

Topics: POC success criteria; baseline sizing; burst pool and limits; autoscale triggers and cooldown; fallback model variants; security/compliance constraints for Private/VPC; timeline and next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right folks, thanks for joining. Quick roll call. Jordan from Redwood, Priya our latency nerd, Samir on the notes.
[00:12] Carlos Mendes: Carlos here. Aisha, Liam, Mei all on. Thanks.
[00:20] Jordan Lee: Great. The agenda — we want to nail success criteria, discuss what baseline reserved capacity looks like, how burst should behave, and fallback policies if we hit capacity limits. Priya, wanna open on the technical framing?
[00:35] Priya Nair: Sure. So hi everyone. Quick framing — for a scoped POC we normally capture three vectors: throughput (RPS/tokens per second), latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99), and quality delta when we do model fallbacks. The important bit for capacity is understanding your steady-state traffic vs peak spikes, and the expected KV cache hit rate because that materially changes GPU memory footprint and per-token latency.
[01:10] Aisha Khan: To be explicit on SLOs — we care about p95 under 250ms for customer-facing completions, p99 below 600ms is desirable but not required. For background processing lower.
[01:22] Priya Nair: That helps, thanks. Do you have a representative traffic profile or a 24-hour trace?
[01:30] Carlos Mendes: We have a day trace — typical weekday has two big peaks around 09:00 and 16:00 UTC. Average concurrent sessions about 800, peak around 1.2k. Token distribution: median 120 tokens, 95th at 800 tokens. We can share the trace.
[01:48] Priya Nair: Perfect. That token distribution means the KV cache hit rate is important. If you can warm prefixes for heavy users we often see 40-60% effective prefix cache hit which lowers GPU cycles.
[02:05] Liam O'Connor: Quick question — when you say KV cache hit, do you mean Redwood's prefix cache, or something we run?
[02:12] Jordan Lee: Redwood's runtime has automatic prefix/K-V cache; it's transparent. Sometimes the transcript shows it as K V cache — customers call it KV or K-V.
[02:22] Liam O'Connor: Got it.
[02:25] Priya Nair: For sizing, given your numbers my back-of-envelope: for steady 800 concurrent with that token distribution, we'd propose baseline reserved of 3x A100-80GB(or equivalent) with an autoscale headroom to 5x reserved and a burst pool of 2 additional GPUs for short spikes. That configuration aims to keep p95 latency in your 180–240ms window with a 40–50% cache hit.
[03:02] Carlos Mendes: 3 reserved + 2 autoscale + 2 burst? Can you clarify what you mean by burst pool vs autoscale?
[03:12] Priya Nair: Yes. We're distinguishing: reserved capacity = GPUs you commit to for the POC (predictable performance, data isolation). Autoscaling = adding more reserved-equivalent instances (scale-out within your reserved/committed pool) when queue or latency thresholds pass; typically these incur lead-time for launching but are within your committed pool. Burst pool = short-lived, higher-cost capacity that can be used for sudden spikes beyond reserved + autoscale; it's priced differently and can be subject to regional availability. For POC we'd use a small burst pool (2 GPUs) with a max continuous use per spike of ~10 minutes to avoid runaway costs.
[03:53] Aisha Khan: For compliance, if burst runs in a different region or on shared hardware, we need to know data residency and encryption behavior. Is burst on our VPC?
[04:03] Jordan Lee: Important callout. For Private/VPC deployments we can ensure all capacity is inside the customer's VPC, including burst capacity provided it's in the same region and on compatible hardware. If we have to use public shared nodes for burst there's an explicit agreement and audit logs; encryption in transit and at rest still applies. We'll flag that in the security doc.
[04:28] Mei Tan: On quality — you mentioned fallback to a smaller quantized model. Can you describe the expected quality delta?
[04:36] Priya Nair: Short answer: expect a small regression that depends on your prompts. We recommend running paired-evals: run your eval set on the full model and the fallback (8-bit or 4-bit quantized) and measure metrics you care about — e.g., exact-match or BLEU/ROUGE or custom semantic similarity thresholds. For many prompt types delta is small (<5% in our internal metrics) but for finetuned or instruction-heavy prompts it can be higher. The POC should include an automated comparison.
[05:08] Carlos Mendes: OK. Let's tie to success criteria — p95<250ms during 24h benchmark, no more than 2% of requests falling back to degraded outputs during steady-state, and end-to-end cost per 1M tokens under our target. If you can set up a bench that measures those three, we can sign off.
[05:30] Jordan Lee: That’s a solid triad. Priya, do you want to run through the proposed autoscale triggers?
[05:36] Priya Nair: Sure. Suggested policy for POC:
- Primary trigger: sustained p95 latency over 220ms for 30s window -> scale +1 GPU.
- Secondary trigger: CPU/GPU queue depth above 75% for 20s -> scale +1 GPU.
- Cooldown: 90s stable under thresholds before scale-down to avoid thrashing.
- Max autoscale: up to 2 additional GPUs beyond reserved, but autoscale uses committed buckets first.
- Burst policy: if autoscale hits max and we still exceed targets, route to burst pool (2 GPUs) for up to 10 minutes per event; notify Slack and create alert.
[06:35] Liam O'Connor: What about startup latency of adding GPUs? If it takes two minutes to spin up we can still miss SLOs.
[06:44] Priya Nair: Good point. Spin-up time depends on configuration and whether warm workers exist. For cold starts we're typically 60–120s. That’s why we use burst to cover immediate spikes, and rely on proactive scale when we see rising queue lengths. Also warm standby instances (pre-warmed) reduce cold start to ~15–30s but cost more. For the POC we can test both: baseline without warm standby and one run with 1 warm standby to compare economics.
[07:18] Aisha Khan: Do you have any recommended thresholds for queue length we should instrument in our SRE stack?
[07:24] Priya Nair: Instrument queue depth per model worker — we suggest alert thresholds at queue length > 50 per worker (or > 75% GPU occupancy), and use average request token length to normalize. We'll share sample metrics mappings for Datadog/Prometheus.
[07:40] Carlos Mendes: On the cost side, please model cost of reserved vs burst. We prefer more reserved if it reduces overall cost even if upfront commit higher. Can you show a 30-day cost projection for different commit sizes?
[07:53] Jordan Lee: We will. Jordan: action item to send a spreadsheet with cost parity for 2/3/4 reserved GPU configs, autoscale/cold-start assumptions, and estimated burst spend under your spike profile.
[08:05] Priya Nair: Another failover is model fallback routing — when latency breaches we can degrade to a smaller variant or to a cached partial result. Order of preference: 1) KV cache first, 2) smaller quantized model, 3) route to alternate region/model if acceptable. We can configure per-route policies so some critical endpoints never fallback.
[08:30] Mei Tan: If we fallback for certain users, how do we track it? We need observability to show percentages by user cohort.
[08:38] Priya Nair: Redwood Console gives per-route and token-level traces; we can tag fallbacks and produce cohort breakdowns. We'll include a sample dashboard.
[08:48] Aisha Khan: Security — SOC two, SSO samel integration and KMS for customer-managed keys. We need to see the audit log format for bursts and fallback decisions.
[08:58] Jordan Lee: We'll share SOC 2 and SAML docs. For KMS we support customer KMS/HSM integrations in Private deployments; with Hosted we can support customer-managed keys for at-rest encryption in many regions. And audit logs include event-level entries for scale events, fallback triggers, and burst consumption.
[09:20] Carlos Mendes: For the 24-hour benchmark, can Redwood run the load from within our region to avoid cross-region variability?
[09:27] Priya Nair: Yes — we'll spin the benchmark runner in your preferred cloud region. We also recommend running two variants: one with warm KV cache for 1 hour prior and one cold-start run to see impact.
[09:38] Jordan Lee: Timeline recap: Priya will draft autoscale policies by Friday (2025-05-09), Jordan will send pricing and cost sheet by Tues (2025-05-12), Carlos to send traces by 2025-05-10, Redwood to run the 24h bench week of 2025-05-12 and share results. Follow-up security deep-dive tentatively 2025-05-15.
[09:58] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. One more question: do you support preemptible or spot GPUs for burst to save cost?
[10:06] Priya Nair: We can use preemptible/spot for burst pools but with caveats: higher preemption risk, possible interruptions — so not recommended for customer-facing synchronous endpoints. For async/background processing it's often a good cost tradeoff. We'll include both pricing options in the spreadsheet.
[10:24] Liam O'Connor: How do we handle model versioning during autoscale — if a new version is rolled do you warm caches?
[10:31] Priya Nair: Rollouts are supported: canary deploys, shard-aware warmups, and automatic fallback to previous stable model if regressions occur. The warm cache won't transfer across different model architectures, so we recommend rolling the model through canary with traffic mirroring to build cache on new instances.
[10:50] Carlos Mendes: For acceptance criteria — we will consider the POC a success if during the signed bench we meet the p95 latency target, less than 2% fallback in steady-state, and the cost per 1M tokens is within 15% of our target. If those hold we move to reserved commit discussion.
[11:06] Jordan Lee: Great. Anything else from Redwood?
[11:09] Samir Patel: Just we'll include a k6 script sample and a template for the prompt set ingestion.
[11:16] Mei Tan: We'll also share a list of endpoints that are critical vs best-effort — that helps scope non-fallback routes.
[11:22] Aisha Khan: Please include an example of the alerting runbook for autoscale triggers. We want clear ops playbooks.
[11:27] Priya Nair: Yep, a simple runbook: alert -> check queue length and recent deploys -> engage burst if running over threshold -> page SRE -> slack incident channel. We'll send a one-pager.
[11:38] Jordan Lee: OK team — we captured action items. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and cost model.
[11:45] Carlos Mendes: Thanks, appreciate the clarity.
[11:48] Jordan Lee: Meeting end.
